title: When Evolutionary Traits Become Dysfunctional
content_html:
When Evolutionary Traits and Psychology Become Dysfunctional

1. Evolution does not optimise for wellbeing. From an evolutionary perspective, psychological and behavioural traits are selected because they increased reproductive success in past environments, not because they reliably promote health or happiness in every context. Traits that were adaptive on average in ancestral hunter–gatherer settings can become maladaptive or “dysfunctional” when the environment changes rapidly. This idea is often described as an evolutionary mismatch: mechanisms tuned for one set of conditions are now operating in a very different world.

2. Evolutionary mismatch: old heuristics in a new world. An evolutionary mismatch occurs when evolved adaptations are expressed in environments that differ substantially from the environments in which those adaptations evolved. Classic examples include a strong preference for sugar and fat—once adaptive under conditions of scarcity, now contributing to obesity and metabolic disease in food-rich modern societies. The same logic applies to many psychological traits: our brains evolved to manage small-scale, face-to-face social groups, simple technologies, and relatively predictable ecological threats, not global media, algorithmic feeds, and 24/7 connectivity.

3. Supernormal stimuli: exaggerating ancestral cues. A related concept is the supernormal stimulus. Ethologists first showed that animals can prefer exaggerated, artificial versions of natural stimuli (for example, birds choosing oversized fake eggs over their own). Contemporary authors have argued that modern human environments are full of supernormal stimuli: ultra-processed foods, vividly coloured packaging, and on-demand pornography present exaggerated versions of cues (sweetness, fat, sexual signals) that our motivational systems evolved to prioritise. These inputs can “hijack” reward circuits, driving repeated consumption in ways that no longer serve long-term wellbeing.

4. Anxiety and the hypersensitive threat detector. Defensive systems such as anxiety illustrate how an adaptive bias can become problematic. From an evolutionary standpoint, it is often better for a threat-detection system to be overly sensitive—producing many false alarms—than to miss a real danger (sometimes called the “smoke detector principle”). In modern, relatively safe environments, this same low threshold for alarm can manifest as chronic anxiety, phobias, or hypervigilance: the system is doing what it was built to do, but the distribution of threats has changed.

5. Reward, addiction, and compulsive behaviours. Dopamine-based reward circuits evolved to attach motivational “wanting” to cues that predicted biologically important rewards such as food, social contact, and sex. In contemporary settings, drugs, gambling technologies, and digital platforms exploit the same prediction-error and incentive-salience mechanisms, often with highly optimised reinforcement schedules. The result can be addictions or compulsive patterns: the underlying circuits are intact, but they are being driven by stimuli far more potent, frequent, or precisely tuned than anything encountered in ancestral environments.

6. Sexual systems and supercharged cues. Human sexual attraction mechanisms evolved under conditions where erotic cues were intermittent, context-bound, and tied to real partners. Today, high-definition pornography, algorithmically personalised content, and stylised advertising can present a continuous stream of highly salient sexual stimuli. Several authors have framed compulsive pornography use and distorted sexual expectations in terms of supernormal stimuli overactivating evolved sex- and reward-related systems. Here again, what looks like “dysfunction” at the personal level can be understood as ancient machinery operating under radically novel conditions.

7. Social cognition, dress, and status signalling. Social perception systems that evolved to read faces, bodies, and status cues in small groups now also process culturally dense signals conveyed by clothing, brands, and stylised self-presentation. Recent work on dress and person perception shows that clothing systematically shapes inferences about personality, competence, and morality. In some cases, this can contribute to maladaptive outcomes: status anxiety, internalised appearance standards, or prejudice based on dress codes, all reflecting evolved social-evaluation mechanisms tuned to a much simpler signal space.

8. Mental disorder as extreme or mismatched adaptation. Evolutionary psychiatry has started to frame many mental disorders as the extremes, side-effects, or mismatches of otherwise adaptive systems. Anxiety, depression, paranoia, and some psychotic symptoms have been interpreted as hypersensitive or context-misaligned expressions of mechanisms that once helped manage threat, social rank, and group cohesion. This does not mean such conditions are “good” or that treatment is unnecessary; it means that understanding their evolutionary roots can suggest new interventions, such as modifying mismatched environmental inputs as well as using pharmacological and psychotherapeutic tools.

9. Plasticity: how development and culture steer evolved systems. Evolved traits are not hard-wired reflexes; they are flexible programs that expect to be tuned by experience. That plasticity is itself adaptive, but it also means early adversity, chronic stress, or distorted cultural messages can push systems toward unhealthy attractors: persistent shame about the body, compulsive validation-seeking, or difficulty regulating desire and threat responses. Environmental pressures that were rare or absent in ancestral settings—such as continuous performance monitoring, social media comparison, and economic precarity—can shape these systems in ways that feel deeply maladaptive to the individual.

10. Summary. Evolutionary psychology does not claim that evolved traits are always beneficial. Instead, it explains why some mental and behavioural patterns recur and why they are so resistant to change: they are implemented by systems that were once useful and that still operate according to ancient design criteria. In rapidly changing, highly engineered modern environments, those same systems can become sources of distress and dysfunction. Recognising this mismatch opens the door to a dual strategy: treating symptoms directly while also redesigning environments—diet, technology, social structures—to be less exploitative of our evolved vulnerabilities.
